exercise.title: Why do logarithms prove the general power rule?

statement.p: For x>0, writing \ln y=r\ln x and differentiating produces y'=rx^{r-1} for any real exponent r. In your own words, why does this argument not need the exponent to be an integer, and why is the proof stated for x>0?

hint.p: The logarithm turns a power into a constant times \ln x. Natural logarithms of real numbers need a positive input.

subsection.title: Hyperbolic sine and cosine
subsection.p: The exponential function has two natural halves: an even half and an odd half.
These are called the hyperbolic cosine and hyperbolic sine.
The names look trigonometric, but the definitions are exponential. That makes their derivatives immediate.
Compare this with sine and cosine:
For hyperbolic functions, the minus sign disappears:

figure.caption: The function \cosh x is even, while \sinh x is odd.

subsection.p: These functions also recombine to give exponentials:
So hyperbolic functions are not new mysteries. They are a useful way to package exponentials symmetrically.

exercise.title: Why is there no minus sign in the hyperbolic cosine derivative?

statement.p: We have (\sinh x)'=\cosh x and (\cosh x)'=\sinh x, unlike the circular pair with a minus on cosine. In your own words, why does that happen from the exponential definitions, and why are hyperbolic functions not a new mystery?

hint.p: Hyperbolic sine and cosine are even and odd combinations of e^x and e^{-x}. Differentiating those combinations never introduces the extra minus that a circular shift produces.

exercise.title: Why is the identity \cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1 a hyperbola rather than a circle?

statement.p: The point (\cosh t,\sinh t) lies on X^2-Y^2=1, while (\cos t,\sin t) lies on X^2+Y^2=1. In your own words, why does that minus sign belong, and why does the same identity help explain a hanging cable?

hint.p: Circular functions live on a circle; hyperbolic functions live on a hyperbola. The catenary check uses 1+\sinh^2u=\cosh^2u to match a force-balance differential equation.

exercise.title: Why does the power formula not automatically settle x=0?

statement.p: The cube root is defined at 0, but its difference quotient becomes unbounded there. In your own words, why must the point x=0 be checked separately, even after the general power rule is known?

hint.p: A formula on x>0 does not decide a two-sided derivative at the origin. The function may exist at 0 while no finite tangent slope exists.

subsection.p: This is a good preview of differential equations. A physical law can describe a curve by a relation among its derivatives. Solving the law means finding a function with exactly that derivative behavior.
Hyperbolic functions are useful because they are built from exponentials and have simple derivative cycles:
They are not just extra names. They package the functions that naturally solve some laws of growth, balance, and shape.
